1.summary: A static variable belongs to the class itself, not to individual objects, so every instance shares one copy. Non-static fields are the per-object ones.

options.A: A separate copy per object describes an instance (non-static) variable.
options.B: Correct: one shared copy exists for the class, no matter how many objects are created.
options.C: static and final are independent modifiers; a static variable does not have to be final.
options.D: Static members can be used from any method, not only constructors.

2.summary: Inheritance flows from superclass to subclass: the subclass acquires the accessible (public and protected, plus package-private in the same package) members of its superclass.

options.A: The direction is reversed: a superclass does not inherit from its subclasses.
options.B: Correct: the subclass reuses the accessible fields and methods declared in the superclass.
options.C: Private members are not accessible to the subclass; it must go through public or protected methods such as getters.
options.D: A subclass in another package still inherits public and protected members.

3.summary: Java allows single inheritance for classes but any number of interfaces, which is how a class can take on multiple types.

options.A: Correct: one superclass, but one or more interfaces.
options.B: A class cannot extend more than one superclass.
options.C: There is no limit on how many interfaces a class implements.
options.D: Only the interface count is unlimited; the superclass count is limited to one.

4.summary: An abstract class may mix abstract and concrete methods and can declare constructors, but it cannot be instantiated directly — a concrete subclass must be created instead.

options.A: An abstract class can contain fully implemented methods; only methods marked abstract lack a body.
options.B: Correct: new is only allowed for a concrete subclass.
options.C: Abstract classes can declare constructors, which subclasses call through super(...).
options.D: Concrete methods are allowed and often provide shared behaviour for subclasses.

5.summary: The final modifier on a class prevents subclassing. The class can still be instantiated and used normally, like String.

options.A: Final classes are instantiable; final simply blocks inheritance.
options.B: Correct: no class may extend a final class.
options.C: Individual methods do not need to be declared final; they are effectively final because nothing can override them.
options.D: Interfaces are unrelated to the final modifier.

6.summary: JComboBox offers constructors with no arguments, an array of items, or a Vector — not three separate String arguments. The array form compiles: new JComboBox<>(new String[]{"Red", "Green", "Blue"}).

options.A: No JComboBox constructor accepts three separate String parameters.
options.B: Correct: the statement fails to compile; pass the items as an array or Vector.
options.C: An array is accepted; the problem is the argument style, not arrays.
options.D: The import affects event handling, not whether this constructor call is valid; the class itself comes from javax.swing.

7.summary: An abstract method only declares a signature; adding a body is a compile error. Either remove the braces and end with a semicolon, or make the method concrete and let subclasses override it.

options.A: Abstract methods cannot have bodies; default bodies are an interface feature, not an abstract-class feature.
options.B: Correct: the valid form is abstract public void display();
options.C: Abstract methods are normally public or protected; they cannot be private because subclasses must implement them.
options.D: The class being abstract does not allow a body on an abstract method.

8.summary: Font(String name, int style, int size) exists, so the declaration compiles and creates a bold 16-point font. The trailing space does not cause an error; an unrecognised family name simply falls back to a default font.

options.A: That constructor does exist: Font(String name, int style, int size).
options.B: Spaces are legal in font names (for example Times New Roman); the string is not rejected.
options.C: Correct: the call is valid, with style Font.BOLD and size 16.
options.D: Font.BOLD is a constant int and is exactly what the style parameter expects.

9.summary: Since Java 8, an interface method with a body must be marked default or static (private helper methods are also allowed since Java 9). A plain instance method with a body does not compile.

options.A: Only default, static, or private methods may have bodies; a plain method cannot.
options.B: Correct: without default or static, the method must be abstract and have no body.
options.C: Interface methods are commonly public; visibility is not the problem here.
options.D: public is not enough — the missing default modifier is the compile error.

10.summary: The parentheses after Rectangle are a syntax error; the valid form is class Rectangle { ... }. Constructors have no return type, and printing inside a constructor is legal.

options.A: Constructors never declare a return type, not even void.
options.B: Correct: remove the () that follows the class name.
options.C: Constructors may contain any statements, including println.
options.D: The constructor body is fine, but the class header does not compile.

11.summary: Each outer iteration prints one row of four characters, with 7 when i < j and 3 otherwise. For i = -2, -1, 0, 1 the rows are 3777, 3377, 3337, 3333.

options.A: Correct: as j increases past i, the printed character switches from 3 to 7, so each row has one more 3 than the row above.
options.B: All 3s would mean i < j was never true, but it becomes true in the later columns of every row.
options.C: This is what you get if the comparison is reversed to i > j.
options.D: This is what you get if 3 and 7 are printed in the wrong branches of the if.

12.summary: A GUI application is built from components placed in containers and arranged by layout managers, with events connecting the interface to the program logic.

options.A: Components are the visible controls the user interacts with.
options.B: Containers hold and group components, and a frame is the top-level window.
options.C: Layout managers decide component positions and sizes.
options.D: Database tables are unrelated to the structure of the interface.

13.summary: JFrame.add() places the component on the frame's content pane; with the default border layout and no constraint, the single button lands in the centre.

options.A: Correct: add() delegates to the content pane of the JFrame.
options.B: This reverses the relationship — a container is added to the button, not the other way round.
options.C: setContentPane() needs a container such as a JPanel; button.getText() returns a String.
options.D: JFrame has no setButton method.

14.summary: Menus form a tree: a JMenuBar at the top, a JMenu for each drop-down (and for each submenu), and a JMenuItem for each command.

options.A: Correct: JMenuBar contains JMenus; the File JMenu contains items and the Print JMenu, which in turn contains its own items.
options.B: The roles are reversed — JMenuItem is a leaf command and cannot hold menus.
options.C: A JMenuItem cannot contain a menu bar; the hierarchy is built the other way around.
options.D: A JMenuBar is required to host the menus at the top of the window.

15.summary: A submenu is a JMenu added inside another JMenu. JMenu extends JMenuItem, so it can sit where an item is expected while still holding its own items.

options.A: A JMenuItem is a leaf command; it cannot contain other items.
options.B: Correct: Print is a JMenu nested inside the File JMenu.
options.C: JMenuBar is the top-level container that holds the menus; it does not represent a submenu.
options.D: JToolBar is a row of buttons and is unrelated to menus.

16.summary: JFrame.setJMenuBar() is the dedicated method that attaches a menu bar to the top of the frame. Adding it to the content pane treats it as an ordinary component.

options.A: add() treats the bar as a normal component in the content area, not as the frame's menu bar.
options.B: Correct: setJMenuBar installs the bar in the frame's menu-bar position.
options.C: JFrame has no setMenu method; AWT Frame.setMenuBar takes an AWT MenuBar, a different legacy API.
options.D: This also treats the menu bar as a regular component instead of using the menu-bar slot.

17.summary: A submenu is a JMenu nested inside another JMenu; its commands are JMenuItems. The Print JMenu is added to the File JMenu like an item.

options.A: Correct: create the Print JMenu, fill it with the two JMenuItems, then add it to the File menu.
options.B: A JMenuItem cannot hold other menus; the entry that opens a submenu must be a JMenu.
options.C: JMenuBar is the top-level bar for the whole window, not a submenu.
options.D: That removes the Print submenu shown in the figure, leaving both items directly under File.

18.summary: In the delegation model the component is the source: it creates an event object and sends it to the listeners registered with addActionListener(). The listener's actionPerformed() runs.

options.A: There is no polling; the source pushes the event to its listeners.
options.B: Correct: the clicked button fires an ActionEvent, and the registered listener handles it.
options.C: Layout managers only arrange components; they do not process input.
options.D: main() is not re-invoked; the event dispatch thread delivers the event to the listener.

19.summary: The model has three players: the source that fires the event, the event object carrying information about it, and the listener whose method gets called.

options.A: The source is the component where the event originates, such as the button.
options.B: The event object carries details about what happened.
options.C: The listener implements the handler method that responds to the event.
options.D: Layout managers arrange components but are not part of the event model.

20.summary: super(name, id, department) invokes the Employee constructor from the Manager constructor, and it must be the first statement in the subclass constructor.

options.A: Without super, this reads as a method call and does not run the superclass constructor.
options.B: Correct: super(...) chains to the superclass constructor with those arguments.
options.C: this(...) calls another constructor in the same class, not a superclass constructor.
options.D: That calls the superclass method displayInfo(), not its constructor.

21.summary: An override keeps the same name, parameter list, and return type. The override can call super.displayInfo() to reuse the superclass output, then print the team size.

options.A: Correct: same signature as the superclass method, with super.displayInfo() called first.
options.B: This is an overload: the different parameter list means Employee.displayInfo() is not overridden.
options.C: A private method cannot override the superclass method; the access is more restrictive.
options.D: The return type must match the superclass method, so returning String is an invalid override.

22.summary: Manager.displayInfo() calls super.displayInfo() first, printing the employee name, ID, and department, then adds the Team Size line.

options.A: Team Size alone would print only if the superclass call were missing.
options.B: Correct: the superclass details print first, then the overriding method adds the team size.
options.C: The employee details alone would print if the override never printed the team size.
options.D: Overriding is exactly what is happening; the code is valid.

23.summary: A blank final instance field must be definitely assigned exactly once by the end of every constructor, which this constructor does.

options.A: Fields get default nulls, but a blank final still needs an explicit assignment; the default does not satisfy the rule.
options.B: Correct: assigning the final field once in the constructor is allowed.
options.C: final can be applied to fields, methods, and classes.
options.D: Final fields may be declared without an initializer and assigned in a constructor.

24.summary: StringBuffer is mutable: append(), insert(), and similar methods modify the same object, avoiding a new String for every change.

options.A: String is the immutable class; StringBuffer is its mutable counterpart.
options.B: Correct: the buffer's contents can change in place.
options.C: StringBuffer stores characters, such as names and departments.
options.D: StringBuffer prints fine; println calls its toString().

25.summary: JComboBox shows the current selection and opens a drop-down list of the remaining choices.

options.A: Correct: a combo box is the standard drop-down selector.
options.B: JList displays all items as a visible list rather than a drop-down.
options.C: JRadioButton is a single option button, not a list of models.
options.D: JTextField accepts typed input and offers no list of choices.

26.summary: A ButtonGroup links the radio buttons so that selecting one deselects the others; without it, any number can stay selected.

options.A: Correct: add each JRadioButton to the same ButtonGroup.
options.B: Without a ButtonGroup the radio buttons are independent and more than one can be selected.
options.C: JCheckBox is designed for independent, multiple selections.
options.D: JMenuItems are menu commands, not a radio-button group.

27.summary: A JLabel shows the title text, JTextFields accept the height and weight, and a JButton triggers the calculation.

options.A: Correct: each component's type matches the role shown in the figure.
options.B: The roles are swapped: labels are not inputs and text fields are not labels.
options.C: The button and label are assigned to the wrong roles.
options.D: Labels, buttons, and text fields are all mismatched here.

28.summary: BorderLayout has five regions; NORTH sits at the top, CENTER fills the middle, and SOUTH sits at the bottom, matching the figure.

options.A: Correct: label NORTH, input area CENTER, button SOUTH.
options.B: FlowLayout places components in one row that wraps, not in top, centre, and bottom regions.
options.C: GridLayout would give every component an equal cell in a single row.
options.D: CardLayout shows one component at a time, like a stack of cards.

29.summary: A JButton fires an ActionEvent; the class implements ActionListener and overrides actionPerformed(ActionEvent) to handle the click.

options.A: Correct: addActionListener(this) registers the class, and actionPerformed runs on each click.
options.B: mouseClicked reports mouse presses and releases, not the button's action.
options.C: ItemListener handles selection changes in components such as combo boxes and check boxes.
options.D: WindowListener handles window events such as closing, not button clicks.

30.summary: getText() returns a String, so Double.parseDouble() converts the typed text into a double before calculating.

options.A: Correct: parse both fields with Double.parseDouble before using them.
options.B: A JTextField is an object; it cannot be assigned to a double.
options.C: A String cannot be assigned to a double without parsing.
options.D: Casting does not convert a String to a double; that cast does not compile.

31.summary: Square the height with parentheses, divide the weight by it, then multiply by 703: weight / (height * height) * 703.

options.A: Correct: the parentheses square the height before the division.
options.B: Without parentheses this is (weight / height) * height * 703, so the height cancels out instead of being squared.
options.C: The height cancels out, leaving weight / 703.
options.D: Multiplying by height squared inverts the formula.

32.summary: Constructors can be overloaded: several constructors are allowed as long as their parameter lists differ. Constructors have no return type, not even void.

options.A: Correct: different parameter lists distinguish the constructors.
options.B: Two constructors with the same parameter list is a duplicate-method compile error.
options.C: A class may declare as many constructors as it needs.
options.D: Constructors never declare a return type.

33.summary: A final method cannot be overridden, though subclasses still inherit it and can call it.

options.A: Correct: final blocks overriding in every subclass.
options.B: final and static are independent modifiers.
options.C: Subclasses can call final methods; they simply cannot override them.
options.D: final applies in every package, not just the same one.

34.summary: The reference type decides which methods are visible at compile time. Vehicle has no drive(), so v.drive() fails to compile until v is cast to Car.

options.A: The compiler only checks the reference type, not the object it points to.
options.B: Correct: use ((Car) v).drive() after confirming the object really is a Car.
options.C: The statement never compiles, so it cannot throw at runtime.
options.D: final has no effect on which methods can be called through a reference.

35.summary: An abstract subclass may leave inherited abstract methods unimplemented; the first concrete class in the hierarchy must implement all of them.

options.A: An abstract subclass may defer them; only concrete classes must implement them.
options.B: Correct: abstract subclasses can pass the obligation further down.
options.C: Abstract methods have no bodies, so nothing is provided to inherit.
options.D: The compiler never invents implementations for abstract methods.

36.summary: private restricts access to the declaring class only; being in the same file or the same package does not grant access. A public getter is required.

options.A: A shared file does not change access control.
options.B: Correct: a is private to Data1 and cannot be read from Main.
options.C: Package access comes from the default (no modifier), not private.
options.D: println prints int values fine; the access is the problem.

37.summary: An array object has only its own members such as length. Data2 methods belong to Data2 elements, so obj2[0] must be assigned an object before a method call.

options.A: An array does not inherit the methods of its element type.
options.B: Correct: call getColor() on obj2[0] after obj2[0] = new Data2(...).
options.C: Arrays can hold object references.
options.D: The array exists already, but its slots are null until elements are created.

38.summary: The loop runs for i = 3 through 7, printing 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. When i becomes 8 the condition i < 8 fails and the loop stops.

options.A: Correct: the squares of 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7.
options.B: 64 would require i = 8, which fails the loop condition.
options.C: The code prints i * i, not i.
options.D: This stops one iteration early; i = 7 still satisfies i < 8.

39.summary: UML generalisation points from the subclass to the superclass with a hollow triangle at the superclass end, so the arrow goes from Cylinder to Circle.

options.A: Correct: hollow triangle at Circle, pointing from the derived class.
options.B: The direction is reversed; the subclass points to the superclass.
options.C: A composition diamond expresses has-a, not inheritance.
options.D: A dashed dependency arrow is not an inheritance relationship.

40.summary: Protected members are directly accessible inside the subclass, so getVolume() can use radius and PI; square the radius, then multiply by the height.

options.A: Correct: PI * radius * radius * height.
options.B: This uses only one radius factor, giving area times height without squaring.
options.C: This squares the height instead of the radius.
options.D: This adds the terms instead of multiplying them.

41.summary: Volume = PI x radius x radius x height = 3.142 x 4 x 4 x 5 = 251.36.

options.B: This is only the circle area, without multiplying by the height.
options.C: This uses PI = 3.14 instead of the class constant 3.142.
options.D: This is PI x radius x height, missing one radius factor.
